claims.text: The balance between configurational entropy and temperature-activated short-range atomic ordering governs whether the nanoparticles remain uniform solid solutions or undergo phase segregation.
Differences in elemental diffusion kinetics and atomic-size mismatch drive temperature-activated short-range ordering.
The initial nanoparticles are homogeneous, near-equiatomic solid solutions containing five or more metals.
Heating within 473–1923 K induces short-range atomic ordering that competes with entropy-driven mixing.
At lower temperatures, high configurational entropy stabilizes the random solid solution.
As temperature increases, differences in atomic size and bonding energy cause differential diffusion and local ordering.
Overcoming the activation barrier for ordering produces ordered clusters or phase segregation.
Ordered clusters or phase segregation undermine structural and chemical uniformity.
If the kinetic barrier to ordering remains high, the nanoparticles retain a disordered structure.
Nanoparticles with a high kinetic barrier to ordering maintain their random solid-solution structure and stable catalytic and thermoelectric properties across 473–1923 K.
Nanoparticles with lower ordering barriers exhibit earlier atomic ordering and phase segregation near the upper end of the temperature range.
Greater atomic-size mismatch or more disparate diffusion rates can lower the effective barrier to ordering.
Maintaining near-equiatomic ratios ensures high configurational entropy.
The prediction applies when configurational-entropy and atomic-ordering contributions are of comparable magnitude.
Dominant surface segregation or other interfacial phenomena can cause deviations from the prediction.
Changes in bonding characteristics caused by particular elemental combinations can cause deviations from the prediction.
Ordering activation energies and operating atmospheres affect the temperature at which ordering begins.
Enhanced atomic-size mismatch is expected to produce a lower ordering barrier than minimal atomic-size mismatch.
Failure of the enhanced-size-mismatch particles to order or segregate by the highest test temperature would falsify the proposed ordering-mediated stability hypothesis.
